evidence.label: Generalized Cartan–Hadamard isoperimetry and Euclidean equality rigidity
Sharp integral fillings in CAT(0) spaces

headline: Proves sharp Euclidean fillings in CAT(0) spaces and claims the generalized Cartan–Hadamard isoperimetric inequality.
scope: Complete simply connected manifolds with sectional curvature at most κ ≤ 0, and integral cycles of dimension 2 and up in proper CAT(0) spaces.
plain: The isoperimetric inequality says a ball has the least boundary area for its volume. The Cartan–Hadamard conjecture says this stays true, or gets stronger, in spaces that curve like a saddle. One paper claims the conjecture in every dimension and for every curvature bound κ ≤ 0. It adds that only flat balls attain the flat bound. A second paper proves a sharp filling bound in CAT(0) spaces, which gives the flat case, and Lean checks it.
doesNot: This does not cover spaces with some positive curvature, where the flat isoperimetric inequality can fail.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: André Weil, whose work began the surface case of the comparison
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a long-standing conjecture of comparison geometry in every dimension; the flat case has a Lean check.

explanation:
Take a unit cube. Its volume is 1 and its surface area is 6. A round ball with volume 1 has radius about 0.620. Its surface area is about 4.836. In ordinary three-dimensional space, every shape of volume V has surface area at least 3 × (4π/3)^(1/3) × V^(2/3). For V = 1 that is the 4.836 of the ball, and the cube's 6 is larger. This is the isoperimetric inequality: among shapes of a given volume, the ball has the least boundary.

A Cartan–Hadamard manifold is a complete curved space with no holes to loop around and sectional curvature at most zero. Sectional curvature at most zero means it curves like a saddle or is flat in every direction. Suppose the curvature is at most some κ ≤ 0. The generalized Cartan–Hadamard conjecture says every region then has at least the boundary area of the equal-volume ball in constant curvature κ[3]. Comparing balls alone does not settle it, because arbitrary regions must be handled. Weil started the surface case in 1926[4]. Kleiner proved dimension three[5], and Croke proved the flat comparison in dimension four[6]. A recent preprint reached the flat comparison in dimensions three through nine[7].

The first paper claims the conjecture in every dimension, for every κ ≤ 0[1]. It covers every set of finite volume and finite perimeter, not only smooth regions. It also claims a rigidity result. If a bounded region meets the flat bound exactly, the region itself is a round flat ball. The space outside it need not be flat[8].

The second paper works in CAT(0) spaces. These are spaces where every triangle is at least as thin as a flat triangle with the same side lengths. It takes a closed n-dimensional cycle, a generalised surface that may have overlapping layers. It proves the cycle bounds a filling of mass at most c_n times the cycle's mass to the power (n + 1)/n[2]. For n = 2, c_2 = 1/(6√π), about 0.0940[9]. A unit sphere has area 4π, about 12.566. Then c_2 × (4π)^1.5 works out to exactly 4π/3, about 4.189, the volume of the unit ball. So round spheres show the constant cannot be improved. As a corollary, the flat Cartan–Hadamard inequality holds in every dimension from three up[10].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of the filling result and of the optimality of its constant. So the second paper proves these, as far as the Lean statements match the paper. Lean does not cover the first paper's curved comparison for κ < 0 or its rigidity result; those are claims. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major. The flat case has a Lean-checked route through the filling paper. The curved case κ < 0 and the rigidity result rest on the first paper alone, without Lean or published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A lower bound on boundary area in terms of enclosed volume, with balls as the best case.
The curvature of a space along each two-dimensional direction; negative means saddle-like.
A complete, simply connected curved space whose sectional curvature is never positive.
A space where every triangle is at least as thin as the flat triangle with the same side lengths.
A generalised closed surface with whole-number layers, allowed to be singular.
A higher-dimensional piece whose boundary is a given cycle.
The total size of a cycle or filling, counting layers.
